0: "A single note can make a place. A second note can change everything about that place."
"How to find notes on a keyboard, what an octave is, how one pitch becomes a musical reference, and how a moving musical voice changes the sound around it."
"By the end, you'll create your own tiny two-voice soundscape."
`Begin with Sound` (scroll/focus section 1). Secondary `Explore the Keyboard` (scroll/focus section 3); don't autoplay.
1: "Imagine stepping into a quiet space. There is only one sound in it. Listen for a moment without trying to decide what it means. Notice its color, texture and the way it fills—or doesn't fill—the space."
Audio caption (shown after playback begins or completes)
"This is C, our home sound for today. C isn't automatically home in all music; we're choosing it as our reference."
"If this sound were a place, what kind of place would it be?"
`A few words or a tiny sketch idea…`
"There's no correct emotional description. Your ears and imagination get to decide."

one user-triggered C3 (MIDI 48) soft drone with pause/stop; 15 seconds initial, optional replay. Show W1-01 learner art, but only after play begins. Nothing in initial visual implies a chord or seven-note scale.
2: "Keep C sounding underneath. Now listen as a higher note enters, stays for a moment, and leaves. Our foundation hasn't moved, but the whole space may seem different."
`Hear E`, `Hear G`, `Hear D`. Each sounds the same C3 drone plus a single independently gated upper tone; show exactly one upper note at a time, and release it while C3 continues briefly.
"That was two simultaneous notes: a held foundation and a moving upper voice. You're already hearing a simple harmonic relationship."
"Which visitor changes the atmosphere most for you? Which one would you like to hear again?"

`Try another note` exposes a selectable C4, D4, E4, F4, G4, A4, B4 row, without stacking them. Label all note names only **after** at least one listen. W1-02 visitor mode, one visible visitor node per example; arrows/positions semitone-accurate.
separate labeled controls and an aria-live status saying `Now playing C with E`, etc. Never make a changing color the only signal.
3: `The keyboard is a map of pitch`

"Move right on a keyboard and pitches rise. Move left and they fall. The white keys use seven letter names—A, B, C, D, E, F and G—and those names repeat. The black keys form groups of two and three, so you can find your way even when you're new to the instrument."
"Find a group of two black keys. The white key immediately to its left is C. Find the next group of two black keys and you've found a higher C."
`Show C landmarks` reveals two correctly placed Cs within W1-06 learner keyboard (C3–C5), with sound on click if audio enabled. `Hide note names` toggles labels; labeled fallback always available.
"Two Cs can be higher and lower but still belong to the same repeating family of notes. The distance from one C to the next higher C is an octave. On this keyboard, an octave spans twelve semitones."
"Play—or click—one C and the next C. Do they feel related even though their registers are different?"

`Find two Cs`; after selection, answer "Yes—both notes are C, one octave apart." Show the note name plus position when revealing. Wrong-answer help: "Look just to the left of each group of two black keys."
C4=60, C5=72; some DAWs use different octave-number conventions, so use MIDI pitch values for any generated sound.
4: "A keyboard is more than a set of buttons. As its pattern becomes familiar, you can start to imagine where a note lives—even when the keys aren't in front of you. Like knowing your way around a familiar neighborhood, this picture helps musical ideas find a place."

1. `Look` — "Notice the two black keys and find C."
2. `Draw` — "Sketch one octave, or trace its shape with your finger."
3. `Hide` — "Hide the labels. Can you still find the same landmarks?"
4. `Imagine` — "Picture, gesture or say where E is. It's fine to keep the keyboard visible if you prefer."
5. `Reveal · Hear · Verify` — "Find E on the real keyboard, hear it, and compare it with what you imagined."
`Reveal the map`; no scoring, speed limit or penalty. This is an original Ploger-informed pedagogy adaptation: refer to the source book in teacher metadata, not as a full interactive replica.
5: `Hear a note before you play it`

"Listen to E above the home sound. Now stop the upper note, but keep C underneath. Can you still hear E in your imagination? You can hum it, whistle it, trace its height with your hand, or simply think about it."
`Listen` → `Imagine` (manual advance, 3-second quiet period if desired) → `Hum or gesture` (no microphone capture) → `Find it` → `Compare`.
"The instrument is here to help you check what you imagined—not to grade you. Hearing, humming and finding are skills that strengthen with practice."
"If the note is hard to hum, just decide whether it sits higher or lower than the one you heard before, and check by listening."
W1-05 learner and SYS-07 process icons. Do not suggest she must hum two pitches simultaneously.
6: "Open your favorite synthesizer or DAW. Start with a soft, sustained C. Choose just two or three upper notes you found interesting. Let them enter in whatever order you wish. One might arrive immediately; another might wait. Keep some space in the music."
"Create a sketch of roughly 15–25 seconds. Before you add at least one note, try to imagine it. Record your sketch and listen back without watching the piano roll."
"Try two versions: one where the second voice enters right away, and one where it waits. Notice how much the musical story changes even when the notes stay the same."
`I've made my sketch` updates only local UI progress (no backend save or upload).
`What changed the feeling most?` freeform, local-only, no transmission; if no note persistence requested, resets on refresh.
"One voice stayed. Another moved. You gave two sounds a relationship—and gave yourself a new way to tell a story."
`Continue to Lesson 1B` (route in index); `Review the keyboard` (returns to section 3). *Do not fabricate integration with, or recording from, her DAW.*

drawers.head: 1A-HIST — History Postcard
fields: `Before the keyboard: finding ways to remember music`

"About a thousand years ago, Guido of Arezzo helped singers learn and remember melodies using an organized approach to musical pitches and syllables. Later medieval traditions used the hand as a guide to singing. The tools have changed, but the question is familiar: how do you turn a sound you hear into something you can remember and share? Our keyboard map is one way to connect musical imagination with a common language."
"Trace an upward musical path with your finger before playing it."
Don't claim Guido invented all music notation or the modern keyboard.

drawers.head: 1A-SCI — Behind the Sound
fields: `Why is a higher C still a C?`

"Most pitched sounds have a main repeating vibration called a fundamental frequency. Double that frequency and you've moved up one octave. Many instruments also produce higher components called overtones, which help give a sound its character. A flute-like pure tone and a shimmering synth pad can play the same C yet sound very different. Pitch and sound color are connected, but they're not the same thing."
"Play one C in two octaves. Then play the same C with two different patches."
Synth sounds may use inharmonic partials; don't state that all overtone patterns are integer multiples.

drawers.head: 1A-AMBIENT — Ambient Composer's Notebook
fields: "In an ambient piece, a quiet sustained note can create the sense of a place. When a higher note enters, it can feel like a visitor stepping into that world. The atmosphere itself hasn't stopped; something has begun to happen inside it. You don't need a busy chord progression to tell a little story. Sometimes two carefully timed voices communicate more than a dozen simultaneous sounds."
"Delay the upper note by five seconds and compare the two sketches."

drawers.head: 1A-REAL — Hear It in Real Music
fields: `Two ways to hear a steady musical place`
"You don't need to name notes in these recordings. Just listen for what stays familiar and what changes."

`Pandit Venkatesh Kumar — Raag Multani (Darbar Festival)` · primary artist/program link https://player.darbar.org/videos/pandit-venkatesh-kumar-raag-multani-music-of-india ; YouTube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WU2_-9P3jY0 **(YouTube watch status not independently confirmed; the Darbar performer/program page is verified and may require a subscription)**.
"The continuing tanpura reference beneath a changing sung melody. This Hindustani performance has its own musical grammar; it isn't an example of our C-major scale."

`Arvo Pärt — Spiegel im Spiegel (performance)` · YouTube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TJ6Mzvh3XCc (YouTube title verified; channel isn't identified as an official artist source). Composition background https://www.arvopart.ee/en/arvo-part/work/544/.
"The piano's repeating tones beside a patient solo line. How little can change while the atmosphere remains recognizable?"
"In your synth, hold one note and change only when a second line enters."
Link to recordings externally, no downloads, thumbnails, autoplay or copied audio.

drawers.head: 1A-WORLD — Musical Worlds
fields: `South India: a raga is more than a row of notes`

"In South Indian Carnatic music, a raga's identity grows from characteristic ways of moving through notes, ornaments and the knowledge of its performers—not simply from an ascending scale. Flutist Jayanth Ambedkar explores Raga Kapi above a tanpura's sustained reference in a recording made near the Tiger Caves in Tamil Nadu. Listen for a steady musical ground and a melodic line that can take many expressive paths without switching Western block chords."
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XI_5A37n4to (unconfirmed watch-page availability; prioritize verified Darbar source).
"Try three little melodic routes over the same synth drone. This is inspiration from a general musical relationship, not a claim to perform Raga Kapi authentically."
Darbar lists the artist as **Jayanth Ambedkar** and describes a Carnatic raga on bansuri; do not label it Hindustani khayal or claim its tuning equals the white keys.

drawers.head: 1A-PAINT · Paint What You Hear
fields: "Listen to the held home note again. If that sound were a place on your canvas, what would it look like? You might choose a wash of color, a shape, a texture or empty space. Now let one higher note enter, and add just one visual gesture to show what changed. The painting belongs to your experience; there is no correct color for C."
"Make a tiny before-and-after diptych: the home note alone, then the same home note with a visitor."
"Look at the two versions, then listen again. Did your drawing help you notice a musical relationship you hadn't heard before?"

"Use paper, paint, a sketchbook, collage or your own digital art tools. You never need to upload your artwork." Reuse blank W1-04 as optional downloadable sheet; no new browser canvas or third-party image assets. This is optional visual expression, **not** the Ploger keyboard-geometry drawing/recall exercise.
